newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China says garrison law won't undermine HK courts.
newsitem.headline: China says garrison law won't undermine HK courts.

text.p: China's plan to try offences committed in Hong Kong by on-duty soldiers in military courts did not undermine the rights of the territory's judicial system, a Beijing-backed newspaper reported on Saturday.
The difference between on and off duty was also plain to see, the Ta Kung Pao quoted legislative bureau director Yang Fukun of China's Central Military Commission as saying.

An on-duty soldier would be acting within professional responsibilities, under orders, and generally in uniform, Yang told a group of Hong Kong deputies to China's National People's Congress (NPC) on Friday.

Hong Kong has been nervous since China stated local courts would have no jurisdiction over offences committed while on duty by Chinese soldiers stationed in the territory after the British colony reverts to Chinese sovereignty in mid-1997.
Off-duty offences would be handled by local courts.

The government has asked Beijing to clarify how jurisdiction would be determined as there were questions about offences committed against civilians whether soldiers were on or off duty -- drink driving while on duty being an example.
NPC delegate Cheng Yiu-tong said Yang explained the difference between on and off duty through the example of an off-duty officer robbing someone after being sent out to deliver a letter.
"It would not then be considered as having happened while on duty because that was not within the scope of the work he was asked to do," Cheng told the South China Morning Post.
